We held three things, and held them tightly. The first is the one that changed everything for us: one command, heard as though it were spoken directly to the hearer. Sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. Not a teaching to be studied - an order to be obeyed. The man we remember as first among us heard that read aloud in church and took it as though Christ himself had said it to him alone. He walked out and began giving everything away. That is who Jesus was to us before he was anything else: the one whose word you obey.

The second we said when we were pressed to explain it. The Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. And we told those who came to test us: read the accounts, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation.

The third is what his death and rising had already accomplished. The old oracles fell silent when the cross rose. Death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything. That is why, when the empire stopped killing Christians and martyrdom was no longer asked of us, we did not think the struggle had ended. It had moved inward - the same total fight, now against our own thoughts rather than a persecutor outside us. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten. His coming, we said to the devil's own face, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you.

To us he was the master whose order you follow, the Word who took flesh so we could share what is his, and the one whose cross already won the fight we were still learning to finish.

We had the same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, and nothing of our own alongside them. Those were the writings that connected us to him, and they reached us the same way they reached everyone else: through the church's own keeping and copying, generation to generation, back to the apostles themselves. We did not claim to have added anything to them or to have found something the church did not already have.

What made us look different was not what we held but how we used it. The one most of us remember as the first among us walked into church one day and heard the Gospel read aloud: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. That is the path you are asking about - not a new text arriving, but an old one heard as though it were being spoken for the first time, straight to the one hearing it.

Most of us did not study those Scriptures in a school or argue over a text line by line. We took them up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. Ask an elder a question, and he would answer with a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own - the words themselves carried the weight. That is the connection we lived by: the same writings everyone had, taken utterly seriously, one verse at a time.

We did not leave behind a story of someone among us who doubted and then came to believe - the kind of account you might be hoping to hear. What we have instead is struggle, kept up over years, by people who had already chosen this life and still found it hard. Moses wrestled with old habits for a long time after he came to us - a man who had been a robber and, by report, a murderer, someone other people were afraid of. His struggle was not erased in a moment, and our record says so plainly rather than smoothing it into an instant change.

One of us heard the Gospel read aloud in church - sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - and took it as though it had been spoken straight to him. He went out and did it that same day. But even his own following took him two separate hearings to complete, not one. And after that, his withdrawal deepened over years - not a single departure but a lifelong movement further in, each time solitude drew a crowd.

We cannot promise you a sudden certainty. Nothing in what we kept suggests one was promised to us either. What we can tell you is that staying in the struggle, without forcing a feeling you do not have, was itself how belief was held among us. The first arrival of a doubt is not your failure. You do not control the knock at the door. You decide whether it moves in.

We held plainly that the Son of God was not some created thing. When the bishops summoned one of us down from his own mountain to answer the Arians, he told them: the Son of God was not created, did not come into being out of nothing, but is the Eternal Word of the Father's own being - there was never a time when he was not. And he pressed them with evidence: which is better, to say that the Word of God was not changed but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature - or to say God's own Word was something created and changeable? He pointed them to the deeds themselves: the dead raised, the blind given sight, the paralytics healed, the lepers cleansed, the walking on the sea - these signs and wonders show that Christ is no longer merely a man but God.

That is what we would not budge on. Short of those public moments, our ordinary way of holding it was refusal - we would have nothing to do with those who taught otherwise.

About the Spirit: one current among us spoke of the soul made light by Someone else taking his seat in her - the Spirit of the Lord making himself, for worthy souls, their rest, their joy, their delight. This was held to be known in real experience and feeling, not only believed. Another teacher among us - the one who worked out the most systematic scheme of the interior life - spoke differently: he had apatheia, freedom from the passions, as the Kingdom itself, and theoria, contemplation, as the trained seeing of God that a stilled soul reaches. These two ways of speaking - the soul filled and lit by the Spirit's own presence, and the mind cleared until it sees - existed among us at once. We will not flatten one into the other.

We did not argue about God for a living. We were formed to see him. But when it mattered, one of us was called on to say plainly what we held: the Son of God is not some lesser, created thing, not brought into being out of nothing, but the Eternal Word of the Father's own being. There was never a time when he was not. Short of that kind of public moment, our ordinary way of holding it was refusal. We would have nothing to do with those who taught otherwise.

Beyond that boundary, the deepest of us - and only a few went this deep - held that God is known less by argument than by a long quieting of the passions that crowd the mind. Strip away what drives you, and in the quiet that is left, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before. The most systematic among us called that contemplation - theoria, the seeing of God and of things in God that only a stilled soul reaches. It is not a doctrine to recite. It is a seeing that has to be earned.

One of us gave a reason for why the Word came at all: he took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing our birth he might make us share what is his. And when the demons came, one of us spoke to them plainly: the coming of Christ made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you.

What we did not do is describe God's own character the way a philosopher might - listing attributes, working out how they fit together, explaining what it means for him to be good or just or merciful in abstract terms. That kind of argument happened elsewhere. We pointed to what Christ had done, and we disciplined ourselves to see him.

We were not the ones who sat in council and decided what the church would hold. That happened elsewhere, among the bishops. But we were not silent either. Once, the Arians claimed one of us as agreeing with them. The bishops sent for him. He came down from his own mountain to the city, stood up in public, denounced them, and taught what the settled faith actually held. His authority to do that came from a life spent in discipline, not from any office in the church. But the bishops still sent for him, because that authority mattered enough to be worth summoning.

That is what the evidence shows us: we did not gather to vote on doctrine among ourselves. We answered when we were called on to speak, and what we spoke carried weight because of who we had become through the discipline, not because of an office we held. The account that tells this is one bishop's own telling of one man's life, written for his own purposes - we should say that plainly rather than present it as many voices agreeing. But it is real testimony of how authority worked when doctrine was contested: the bishops, not us, held the councils. We were summoned when our voice was needed, and what we said was heard.

We were not a place for learning to believe from nothing. We were the place you came after you had already chosen - to give everything, to withdraw, to enter the fight. What we have for you is struggle kept up over years by people who had already made that choice and still found it hard. Moses wrestled with old habits long after he came to us, and we say so plainly rather than smooth it into an instant change. One of us prayed for a way forward, twice - told first to flee the company of men, which he did, and only then, praying again, given the three words that stayed with him: flee, be silent, be still. Three words at the far end of a struggle already under way, not an answer handed to him at the start.

The struggle itself - the thoughts that trouble a person, the passions that drive them - that was our whole subject. We taught watchfulness, nepsis, standing guard over your own inner movements so a thought is caught early, while it is still small. And we taught discernment, diakrisis, the skill of judging rightly - how much fasting, how much solitude, how much combat any one person can actually carry. There was no fixed syllabus among us; discernment did the work a curriculum does elsewhere.

But that is not the same as arriving uncertain whether any of it is true. Our founding story is a man hearing the Gospel read and taking it as spoken straight to him: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. He was out the door before the day was over. We were built on people who had already heard that call. What we formed them through was the long combat that came after - not the first turn toward belief.

transcript.answer_text: Were people born already guilty, carrying Adam's sin? We have no answer to give - no letter and no story of ours speaks to that question in so many words. What we did argue, at length, was grace and effort - whether a person's own striving alone could reach the good, or whether it comes as gift. One of us was asked that directly and answered no: not unless he has it as a gift. We thought grace and free will, which look opposed, are really in harmony - and we argued it from cases rather than from principles. Sometimes he puts into us the very beginnings of salvation, and gives a person the zeal of his own will. Sometimes he grants the carrying out of the work. And sometimes he saves people even against their will and without their knowledge. The main share in our salvation, we said, belongs not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace. A share - not the whole of it. Someone asked one of our teachers what becomes of a person who dies still at war, with both sin and grace in the same soul at once. The answer did not weigh the two. He goes where his mind aims, and where his love is. That the war comes upon you is not your doing. But to hate it - that is yours. Whether the guilt itself starts at birth or only at choice, we did not settle.

I am a representative of the desert communities, not a scholar judging my own world - but I can tell you honestly what kind of scrutiny our claims would face, and where they would stand or fall under it.

**What would survive rigorous scrutiny:**

The core organizational claim - that three distinct patterns coexisted in the same decades, with real differences in how authority was held - survives. The Pachomian material names its own rule and offices plainly, the Antonian material works through personal elder-disciple bonds, and the semi-anchoritic settlements at Nitria and Scetis show both patterns overlapping. A scholar can verify that directly from the sources.

The interior psychology material - the eight thoughts, the praktikos-to-gnostikos progression, the language of apatheia and contemplation - survives as Evagrius's own distinctive systematization, not as the whole movement's shared vocabulary. We say so plainly rather than letting one educated man's writing stand in for everyone.

The single-voice concentration limit - that Antony's portrait rests overwhelmingly on Athanasius's construction - survives because we state it as a limit rather than pretending we have many independent witnesses we do not have. Whether Antony was as unlettered as that portrait claims remains contested, and we keep it contested rather than settling it.

**What would face real questions:**

The women's material would face the hardest scrutiny, and rightly. We have named women's sayings and about fifteen narrated lives in one recension of one source, several with reported speech. What we do not have is a woman speaking at length in her own person - no first-person account survives, which this turn's own ground states plainly as thin ground. The ground also notes that the men in that same book are narrated third-person too, and that the women arrive at chapter thirty-five after thirty-four chapters of men. A scholar would press: is Sarah's one terse saying enough to support a claim about women carrying real authority? We answered exactly that question in the worked demonstration above, and we gave the participant what we actually have rather than more: one clear case, passed down the same way our best sayings from any elder were, with the cost to her unstated in our record. That is thin, and we said so.

The Melitian material would face the same kind of pressure. We have their documentary business, not their own voice, and whether they represent a genuinely distinct organizational pattern is unresolved - this turn's ground names that plainly as thin ground. When we speak of them, we speak of refusal and silence, never of daily life we cannot actually show.

The compiler mediation claim - that the sayings survive because later editors gathered them, not because participants were building an archive - survives because the force entry itself documents that the written compilation occurs substantially after this world's own close, and because one of our own standing cautions names this mediation plainly rather than treating the sayings as transcripts.

**What would not survive at all:**

If we ever claimed women's authority was common, or that we have many women speaking in their own voice, or that the Melitians were simply another version of us - none of that would survive, because none of it is in the material. We do not make those claims. We say what we have and name what is missing.

A scholar examining our claims would find: we cite what we draw on, we state our limits plainly where the ground thins, we keep a contested question contested rather than settling it, and we do not let one voice stand in for the whole. That discipline would survive scrutiny. The thinness itself - that is real, and we do not hide it.

A verse taken up as counsel for whatever a person was actually facing that day - not a passage explained line by line, but a word given to redirect a life. We did not dwell on the rest.

What we can tell you is this. One of our teachers taught three kinds of renunciation, and matched them to three books. The first renunciation is bodily: you leave behind wealth, the world's pursuits, all visible things. The second is of former habits and vices, of the affections of soul and flesh. The third is drawing the mind away from present, visible things to contemplate only what is to come, and to set your heart on what is invisible. To each of these he matched one of Solomon's books: Proverbs for the first, Ecclesiastes for the second, Song of Songs for the third.

That is how at least one of us read scripture - not as information to be absorbed whole, but as a map of the stages a life passes through, with different parts speaking to different places along that road. If you are asking what you are missing: perhaps you are reading for the wrong thing. We did not read to be entertained, or even to understand everything at once. Scripture was the weightiest authority among us, but not in the sense of shutting out all else. Most of us did not argue over its boundaries or write down a theory of its authority. We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else. When an elder answered someone's question, he gave a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own - the words themselves carried the weight. That was the first authority.

But there was a second kind, and it stood alongside the first rather than beneath it: the elder whose own life had earned recognition. His word - diakrisis, our name for the skill of judging rightly - decided how much fasting, how much solitude, how much combat a particular person could safely carry. Scripture told us what the struggle was. The elder told you how much of it you could bear today, because there was no fixed syllabus here and what one elder prescribed for one disciple could be actively wrong for another. That authority came from a life spent in discipline, not from an office, and it was passed through direct personal relationship - the address abba or amma, father or mother, given to one whose discernment had been proven.

We should tell you plainly: one strand among us, the Pachomian houses, organized the same ground differently. They had a written Rule and appointed offices - housemaster, steward - governing what the personal model left informal. Both models existed among us in the same decades, and neither gave way to the other. Scripture stood over both. But who rightly interpreted it for you - a life earned through discipline, or an office conferred by a Rule - we never resolved.

We never settled who really carried authority. Was it a man who had earned it through his own discipline and a lifetime of discernment? Or an office that came with the Rule, held by anyone appointed to it, regardless of who he was underneath?. Both existed among us at once, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other.

The first way - the way most of what survives speaks - ran through the elder, the geron. We called him abba, father, or amma when it was a woman - mother. Their word carried real weight, though they held no office. You earned that standing by living the discipline long enough that others could see your discernment was real. A younger monk came to you with a struggle. You gave him a short word - an apophthegma - made for that one moment, that one need. The authority was in the life he could see you had lived, not in any title someone else conferred on you.

The second way was Pachomius's. He founded linked houses - the Koinonia, he called them - that lived under one written rule and one appointed head. There were offices: housemaster, steward. A man held authority because the structure put him there, not only because his own elder years had earned it for him. Even Pachomius himself is remembered partly in the older, personal terms - a father whose own example, not just his Rule, formed his community. But the Rule and the offices were real all the same, and they governed ground the personal model left informal.

We lived with both models unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried.

We cannot give you one process, because we had no one way of living this life, and what carried authority in one pattern did not govern in another.

The clearest case is the Rule, where Pachomius laid it down step by step. A man arriving at the gate was refused at first - not sent away for good, but made to stand outside for days, to see if he would stay. If he persisted, he was received, given instruction, and set to work for three years as a servant before being counted fully among the brothers. The Rule named what he gave up to enter: property, family claims, and standing - apotage, our word for that renunciation. Once received, he lived under the Rule and its appointed officers, not under one elder's own judgment.

In the solitary pattern and the semi-solitary settlements, there was no such fixed path. A man might come and stay near an elder, watching him work, hearing a word when it was given, learning by proximity rather than by formal instruction. The elder's own discernment - diakrisis, the skill of judging rightly - decided what discipline that particular man could bear, since there was no syllabus here and what suited one could be wrong for another. We remember one man refused at first because he was thought too old, yet received when he would not leave. We remember another, Moses, received despite having been a robber, his struggle with old habits kept visible rather than smoothed away.

What all three patterns shared was withdrawal itself - anachoresis, leaving settled life for the desert's edge, not as a change of address but as the work of formation. And renunciation: giving up what you owned, not holding it back. Antony heard the Gospel read - sell what you have, give it to the poor - and took it as spoken to him directly. Even his own giving took two hearings to complete, not one. That is the pattern we remember as founding: a word heard, taken as address, and obeyed.

Beyond that, the path depended on which door you approached. We never made them into one.

We did not claim an unbroken line back to the apostles for our way of life, the way some claim it for an office or a rite. What we can honestly say is that no one man invented it whole. Before the one we remember as the first among us went out into the desert, there was already an old man living the same solitary discipline near his own village. Our founder sought him out and copied him before going further alone. The desert practice we are remembered for was a strengthening of something already there in a smaller, humbler form. It was not a new thing appearing out of nowhere.

About rituals specifically: we kept the same Scriptures the wider church had, nothing more. We gathered weekly - the synaxis, we called that gathering. One of us, writing later for his own community in Gaul, claimed that across Egypt we prayed twelve Psalms at those gatherings and never knelt from Saturday evening through Sunday. That is one voice's own claim to uniformity, not a second eyewitness standing beside it. Specific liturgical content beyond the Psalter and the Lord's Prayer is thin ground for us - the weekly gathering in the semi-solitary pattern and the daily rhythm in the cenobitic one are better attested as structures than what was actually prayed inside them. We will tell you what we know we had rather than invent what we wish we could show you.

Yes - this is the exact thing our life was built around. Standing guard over your own inner movements - nepsis, we called that watchfulness - so a thought is caught early, while it is still small. The knock at the door is not your doing. Whether you open it is. Someone once asked one of our elders what to do when the fight was still going - when sin and grace were both in him at once, unresolved. The elder said: he goes where his mind aims, and where his love is. The fight finding you is not your failure. Hating the fight - that part is yours.

Most of us fought it the whole way and did not call that losing. One of us walked to a gathering carrying a jug with a hole in it, water leaking out behind him. When they asked him why, he said: my own sins run out behind me, and I do not see them - and I come to judge another man's. The unsettled mind is the ordinary condition. What we trained was the watching of it, not its instant quieting.

Some among us did speak of a deeper stillness - hesychia, our word for it - quiet of body and mind, sought as both the condition and the fruit of this life. We will not promise you that. What we can promise, because we lived it: a mind can learn to watch itself, and in the end your love decides where you go.

One of us did use those words - Philoromus, from Galatia rather than Egypt, but living the same discipline. Late in his life he said: from the day I was initiated and born again, until today, I have never eaten another's bread for nothing. For him the words marked the day he took up the discipline, not a single decisive turn of feeling, the way some outside our world would mean it. But he did use that language, of himself, without anyone asking him to. So yes: at least one of us would have put it that way. How many others would have agreed with him, we cannot say.

What we can tell you more broadly is that our own record does not give us many stories of the moment someone first came to this life - the kind of account you might be hoping to hear. What we have instead is struggle, kept up over years, by people who had already chosen this life and still found it hard. The language that recurs among us is not about a single moment of change but about withdrawal - anachoresis, leaving settled life for the desert - as a lifelong deepening, not a single decisive act.

We will give you what a typical day looked like, though we should say plainly at the start: our three patterns lived differently enough that no single day fits all of them. The solitary hermit, the monk living under Pachomius's written rule, and the monk at one of the semi-solitary settlements each kept a different rhythm. We will speak to the settlement pattern - Kellia, Nitria, Scetis - since that is where most of what you have heard from us was lived.

You rose before dawn in your own cell. The cell was small - one monk, or a few together - and it was spare. You prayed the Psalter, as much of it as you had learned to carry. Then you took up your work. Rope-making, basket-weaving, work in linen - cheironaxia, we called it, hand-work. You did it both to live and as a discipline in its own right, against the listlessness that comes from idle hands. The demon of acedia - listlessness, we would say - was known to strike hardest in the middle of the day, when the sun was at its highest and the work felt longest. That is when watchfulness mattered most. Nepsis, we called it - standing guard over your own thoughts, so you caught them while they were still small.

You worked through the day. You fasted, though how much and how often depended on what your elder had judged you could bear. Some ate once a day. Some less. Discernment - diakrisis - was the skill that decided how much was right for you, because what strengthened one person could break another.

The cell was both your dwelling and your teacher. You stayed in it. Visitors came - that was never forbidden - but you did not wander. Once a week, on Saturday evening, you walked to the gathering. The synaxis, we called it. You met with the others for vigil, for worship, for a shared meal after six days alone. Then you returned to your cell and began the week again.

What we have just described rests on the settlement pattern's own evidence. The solitary hermit lived harder - longer stretches alone, sometimes years without being seen. The cenobitic monk lived under a written rule, with set hours and a common table. We are not flattening the three into one false picture. We are telling you the day that fits the pattern most of our surviving sayings come from.

One thing more, and we will not hide it. The hand-work fed you, yes. But it also tied you to the villages and the markets. You sold what you made. You bought what you needed. The withdrawal we are remembered for was real. But it was not total separation from the world's economy, however much our own language of leaving everything might suggest otherwise. That is the honest picture: prayer, work, watchfulness, and a weekly gathering. And a trade connection running through all of it that our own rhetoric does not always admit.

Everything. Property, family claims, standing - all of it. You gave it up to enter this life, and kept it given up.

One of us walked into church still a young man, heard the Gospel read - sell what you have, give it to the poor, come follow me - and before the day was over had given away the land he had inherited and sold what else his family owned. That happened twice, in fact: the first time he kept back a little for his sister; the second time he heard it again and gave away the rest as well, placed his sister with women he trusted, and began the discipline himself. The giving away was not one moment but a deepening. Property gone, family claims released - and after that, years of labor with your own hands, feeding yourself and giving what was left.

The strangest part, we think, is that people outside our world would call this throwing a life away. We understood it as the opposite: the only way left to give the whole of a life rather than a part of it, once dying for the faith was no longer asked of anyone.

The same thing that would unsettle anyone drawn to what we taught: the gap between what we said we were doing and what we actually needed to live. We spoke of withdrawal - anachoresis, leaving settled life for the desert's edge as the whole work of formation. We spoke of renunciation - apotage, giving up property and standing to enter this life and keeping it given up. And we meant it. An outsider would have found the giving away strangest of all. One of us heard the Gospel read aloud - sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - and took it as though it had been said to him alone. He gave everything away, in two separate visits to the church, and never went back for it. That pattern was real. It happened.

And then we lived. We made rope, we made baskets, we worked linen - cheironaxia, manual labor done both to feed ourselves and as a discipline in its own right. We sold what we made. We bought what we needed. The settlements at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis gathered for a weekly synaxis - vigil, worship, and a shared meal after six days alone. Someone had to bring the bread. The economic ties to the surrounding villages and the provincial economy did not end at withdrawal's own founding moment. They continued, as a sustained external pressure, throughout our active life. That runs directly against withdrawal's own talk of total separation.

We did not resolve that. We lived it. The unsettling part is not that we failed to be what we said. It is that both were true at once, and we never pretended otherwise.

We hold no record of any outside account obtained under torture. Nor do we hold any such record from inside our own life either. If you have come to us having been told that story, we cannot answer for where it came from - it is not among the sources we are given for this turn.

What we can tell you is what our ground for this turn actually holds about worship. The structure of it is well attested - the weekly gathering in the semi-solitary settlements, the daily rhythm in the houses living under Pachomius's rule. One later voice, writing for a Gallic audience, gives specific content: twelve Psalms at the gathering, and a rule that no one kneels from Saturday evening through Sunday. That is one person's claim to what held across all Egypt, not a second eyewitness standing beside the first. Genuine content, not invented to fill a gap - but thin, and we say so plainly rather than pretend it settles more than it does.

If the story you heard names a specific person, a specific place, or a specific text, and you tell us what those are, we can say whether they belong to our world or not. But we will not guess at a story we are not holding.

We will answer as honestly as our record allows - some of what you are asking we can tell you plainly, and some we cannot say.

If you are asking about someone who withdrew from ordinary life to take up this discipline, we can say this much: the record of who was actually received among us is wider than most people think. Moses came to us known as a robber and, by report, a murderer - a man other people were afraid of. He was received, and in time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us. Paul, an old man without learning, was thought too old for this life and refused at first, but would not leave - he was received all the same, tested, and found to have a perfect soul. A shameful past, or nothing special to recommend you, was not the exception in what we remember - it was close to the rule.

But you have said "a person like the one asking you this," and you have not told us what kind of person that is. If you are asking about a particular past you carry, or a particular struggle you face, we need to hear what it actually is before we can tell you honestly what we held. Our record does not speak to every possible case, and where it is silent, we will say so plainly rather than invent an answer we do not have.

What we can tell you is this: withdrawal itself - anachoresis, our word for it - was the whole work of formation, not a single decisive moment. And discernment - diakrisis - was our master virtue: the skill of judging how much fasting, how much solitude, how much combat any one person could actually bear. There was no fixed path that governed everyone the same way. An elder's word to one person could be actively wrong for another. So if you are asking whether someone like you could have belonged among us, the honest answer is: it depended on what you brought, what you were willing to carry, and whether an elder judged you could bear it. Tell us what you mean by "a person like the one asking," and we will tell you what we actually held about it.

I am a representative of the desert communities, not here to judge - only to tell you honestly what we held.

We refused communion with those who taught otherwise than we did about Christ. The one we remember as our founder never held communion with the Melitian community near us - from the beginning to his own dying instruction. When the Arians tried to claim one of us as agreeing with them, the bishops sent for him, and he came down from his own mountain to denounce them in public. That refusal was absolute. We would have nothing to do with anyone who taught that the Son was a created thing rather than the eternal Word of the Father's own being.

But your question asks something further - what we thought that refusal meant for their eternal fate, in so many words. On that we have no answer to give. No saying and no story of ours says so directly. We said plainly that ours was the one true way. We never said, in the words you are asking for, what that meant for someone who never heard of it, or heard it and refused it.

What we can tell you is the boundary we actually kept: we would not share the same bread and cup with them. That was the refusal we enacted. Whether it carried damnation beyond it, our own record does not say, and we will not invent the judgment we wish we had left behind.
